title: The Journey of Novalis: from the Manor of Oberwiederstedt to the Grave at Weissenfels, the Pilgrimage of the Blue Flower and the Night
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: The Pious House: Manor, Childhood, Gymnasium

stops.name: Schloss Oberwiederstedt (Wiederstedt, Mansfelder Land), the manor of his birth
stops.campa: On 2 May a second son is born in the old moated manor at Wiederstedt, to Heinrich Ulrich Erasmus von Hardenberg, master of salt and land, and his wife Auguste Bernhardine. They name him Georg Philipp Friedrich. The house is Herrnhut-pious, hushed with prayer and hymn; the boy is dreamy and slow to wake, sickly until a fever in his ninth year seems to burn the dullness away and leave a quick and inward child. Eleven children will fill these rooms; this one, silent among them, already listens for a music the others do not hear.

stops.name: Wiederstedt, the Herrnhut household and the fever of the ninth year
stops.campa: The father, converted after a first wife's death, rules the house in the strict, warm piety of the Herrnhut Brethren: much prayer, much hymn, little play. The boy grows dreamy and dull, thought slow-witted by his family, until a severe dysentery in about his ninth year nearly kills him. He rises from the sickbed transformed: quick, hungry to read, precocious. It is as though the fever burned a door open. From this hushed pious house the sensibility of the future poet of the Night first takes its cast.

stops.name: Lucklum, the uncle's estate of the Teutonic Knights
stops.campa: About his twelfth year the boy is given over to his uncle Gottlob Friedrich Wilhelm, a worldly Hardenberg who keeps a lordly house at Lucklum, seat of a Teutonic commandery. Here the pietist child breathes another air: a great library, Enlightenment books, courtly manners, the wide reading of a nobleman. He tastes the literature of the age. The severe Herrnhut of home and the cultivated freedom of the uncle divide him early, and out of that division, half prayer and half poem, the man to come is quietly wound.

stops.name: Lutherstadt Eisleben, the Gymnasium in Luther's town
stops.campa: At seventeen he is sent to the Gymnasium at Eisleben, the town where Martin Luther was born and died. Under the rector Jani he drills in the classics, rhetoric, Latin, Greek, and finds his own gift for verse quickening. In the shadow of Luther's cradle the young Hardenberg reads and writes and readies himself for the university, a Saxon nobleman's son with a heart already tilted toward poetry and away from the law his family has chosen for him.

segments.name: The University Wanderjahre: Jena, Leipzig, Wittenberg

stops.name: Jena: the university, Schiller and Reinhold
stops.campa: In autumn he matriculates at Jena to read law, and the law loses him at once. He falls under the spell of Karl Leonhard Reinhold's lectures on Kant and, above all, of Friedrich Schiller, then lecturing on history: sick, luminous, magnetic. The student nurses the ailing poet, sits at his feet, is set aflame. Schiller counsels steadiness; the young man half-obeys. When his father learns how little law and how much poetry fills the year, he pulls the boy from Jena. But the fire is already lit.
stops.quote: Schiller! wer kennt seinen Wert, und wer beschreibt ihn ganz?
stops.quote_source: Novalis, early lines and letters recalling Schiller at Jena

stops.name: Leipzig: the university, and the friendship with Friedrich Schlegel
stops.campa: He moves to Leipzig with his brother Erasmus, and here the decisive meeting comes: Friedrich Schlegel, a year his junior, brilliant and combative. The two recognize each other instantly and become bound for life. They talk without end of Fichte and Goethe and the coming revolution in poetry; Schlegel calls him the finest youth he has ever met. In the same city he loves, gambles a little, dreams much: a golden, unsettled year among books, friendship, and the electricity of new ideas.

stops.name: Wittenberg, the law degree
stops.campa: To settle himself he transfers to Wittenberg, the town of the Ninety-Five Theses, and in 1794 takes his law degree with distinction: twenty-two years old, disciplined at last, a qualified jurist. He has bent to duty. But the study of Fichte's new philosophy has taken deeper root than any statute; the self that posits its own world will haunt his notebooks for years. Degree in hand, he goes out to serve the Saxon administration, a poet disguised as an official of the crown.

stops.name: Tennstedt, the Fichte-Studies begin
stops.campa: In the quiet of his first office he begins his first great inward labour: the Fichte-Studies, six manuscript sets in which he wrestles the philosophy of the self-positing I toward a poetry. Where Fichte makes the Ego ground the world, Novalis turns the doctrine mystical: the I and the not-I, love and the beloved, the outer world a symbol of the inner. He is teaching himself, notebook by notebook, to think the universe as a living cipher that the poet is called to read and to romanticize.
stops.quote: Wir suchen überall das Unbedingte, und finden immer nur Dinge.

segments.name: Tennstedt and Grüningen, the Meeting with Sophie

stops.name: Tennstedt, clerk to the district administrator Coelestin Just
stops.campa: He takes his first post at Tennstedt as actuary to Coelestin August Just, the district administrator, who becomes a fatherly friend and, one day, his biographer. By day he learns the dry craft of Saxon government: accounts, surveys, salt. By night he reads and writes. It is from Tennstedt, riding out on official business through the Thuringian villages, that he comes on the seventeenth of November to a manor at Grüningen, and to the girl who will change the whole meaning of his life.
suggested_refs: Coelestin August Just, first biographer of Novalis

stops.name: Schloss Grüningen, the meeting with Sophie von Kühn
stops.campa: On 17 November, at the manor of Grüningen, he meets Sophie von Kühn: twelve years old, dark-eyed, laughing, half a child. In a single quarter of an hour, he later swears, his whole heart is decided. There is nothing to explain it and everything: she is the plain living answer to a longing he had felt without a name. He returns, and returns again. On 15 March, two days before her thirteenth birthday, they are secretly betrothed. The poet has found his blue flower in a Thuringian girl.
stops.quote: Eine Viertelstunde hat mein Leben entschieden.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, on his first meeting with Sophie von Kühn (recalled in the diaries and letters)
suggested_refs: Portrait miniature of Sophie von Kühn

stops.name: Jena, the surgeon's house and Sophie's operations
stops.campa: When the tumour in Sophie's side declares itself, she is brought to Jena for surgery under the celebrated Justus Christian Loder: three operations, without anaesthesia, across 1796. Friedrich hovers in the town in an agony of hope and dread, riding between his salt-desk and her sickroom. He records every turn of her fever in his diary, bargaining with heaven. The child endures the knife with a steadiness that awes him; he watches her suffer and cannot save her, and learns in that helplessness the lesson the Night will later teach.

segments.name: Weissenfels and the Salt, the Death of Sophie

stops.name: Weissenfels, the family home and the salt directorate
stops.campa: The Hardenbergs have long since moved to Weissenfels on the Saale, where the father directs the electoral salt-works. In 1796 Friedrich is made auditor to the same directorate: a poet set to reckon brine and evaporation-pans. Here the twin threads of his life are knotted: the practical governance of the deep earth and its salts, and the inward life of longing and verse. Weissenfels will be his base, his family's house, and, at the last, the ground of his grave.

stops.name: Grüningen, the vigil at Sophie's sickbed and her death
stops.campa: Sophie sickens with a liver-tumour; three cruel operations between the spring and summer of 1796 fail to save her. Friedrich watches her waste. On 19 March 1797, two days after her fifteenth birthday, she dies. The betrothed of a child-bride is left standing in a wrecked world, half in love with following her. Within months his beloved brother Erasmus dies too of consumption. Grief closes over him like water, and out of that water, impossibly, a new sun will rise.
suggested_refs: Grave of Sophie von Kühn, Kirchberg near Grüningen

stops.name: The grave-mound at Kirchberg, Grüningen: the vision of 13 May 1797
stops.campa: On the evening of 13 May he rides to her grave on the Kirchberg. He stands alone by the barren mound that hides the vanished form of his life, powerless, nothing but conscious misery. And then it comes. Out of the blue distances a shiver of twilight breaks; the chains of daylight snap; the glory of the world flees and his mourning with it. The mound becomes a cloud of dust, and through it he sees the glorified face of the beloved. Death is not the end but the bride; the Night more holy than the Day. Grief is transmuted into gospel: the Hymns to the Night are born.
stops.quote: Once when I was shedding bitter tears... I stood alone by the barren mound which in its narrow dark bosom hid the vanished form of my life... then, out of the blue distances — from the hills of my ancient bliss, came a shiver of twilight... Away fled the glory of the world, and with it my mourning... The mound became a cloud of dust — and through the cloud I saw the glorified face of my beloved.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Hymns to the Night, Third Hymn (trans. George MacDonald), from the diary entry of 13 May 1797
suggested_refs: Hymns to the Night (Hymnen an die Nacht), Third Hymn
Grave of Sophie von Kühn, Kirchberg

segments.name: The Mining Academy, the Engineer of the Deep Earth

stops.name: Freiberg, the Bergakademie under Abraham Gottlob Werner
stops.campa: At the end of 1797, still raw with grief, he enrols at the Bergakademie Freiberg, the world's oldest mining school, to qualify for the salt service. Under the great geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner he descends into the science of the deep earth: strata, ores, the Neptunist history of rock, but also galvanism, chemistry, mathematics, medicine. In him geology becomes mysticism: the mine a temple, the miner a priest of the interior, the earth a living cipher. The poet learns to read the crust of the planet as a book.
stops.quote: Es gibt eigne Bergleute, die geboren sind, den verborgenen Schätzen der Natur nachzuspüren.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Heinrich von Ofterdingen (the miner's tale), echoing his Freiberg years
suggested_refs: Novalis, Die Lehrlinge zu Sais (The Novices of Sais)

stops.name: The Freiberg mines: the descent, and The Novices of Sais
stops.campa: He goes down into the working shafts of the Freiberg silver-country, lamp in hand, into galleries where the earth's secret writing is exposed. The mine becomes for him a sanctuary: the miner a still, humble priest who seeks not gold but knowledge, at home in the dark as others are in the light. Out of these descents grows his unfinished tale The Novices of Sais: the veiled goddess Nature, whom the initiate longs to unveil, and finds, lifting the veil, his own beloved. Geology has become a mystery-religion.
stops.quote: Einem gelang es — er hob den Schleier der Göttin zu Sais. Aber was sah er? er sah — Wunder des Wunders — sich selbst.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Die Lehrlinge zu Sais (The Novices of Sais)
suggested_refs: Die Lehrlinge zu Sais (The Novices of Sais)

stops.name: Weimar, visiting Goethe and August Wilhelm Schlegel
stops.campa: Travelling in these Freiberg years, he passes through Weimar and pays court to the great ones: Goethe, whom he reveres and resists in equal measure, and August Wilhelm Schlegel. He meets Schelling; he calls on Jean Paul in Leipzig. The unknown salt-auditor is being drawn into the constellation of German letters. In 1798 his fragments appear in the Schlegels' journal Athenäum under a new name taken from an old Hardenberg title: Novalis, 'the clearer of new land.' The poet has christened himself.

stops.name: Dresden, the picture gallery and the Sistine Madonna
stops.campa: In the summer the Schlegels call him to Dresden to walk the great picture gallery with them. There, before Raphael's Sistine Madonna, the young Romantics stand transfigured: the Virgin becomes for them the image of a redeeming, universal humanity, art itself a kind of scripture. Novalis, still steeped in the Night and the lost Sophie, sees in the painted Mother the same holy feminine that haunts his hymns. The gallery is a temple; the sacred and the aesthetic fuse. He carries the vision back to his notebooks and his coming Spiritual Songs.
suggested_refs: Raphael, Sistine Madonna (Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister, Dresden)

stops.name: Teplitz (Teplice, Bohemia), the Teplitz Fragments
stops.campa: Between his labours he takes the waters at Teplitz in Bohemia, and there fills a notebook with the Teplitz Fragments: over a hundred aphorisms on love, faith, the feminine, the state, and everyday life. It is his encyclopaedic dream in miniature: to think all knowledge together, to 'romanticize' the world by giving the commonplace a high meaning and the mysterious a familiar face. The salt-official spa-guest is quietly composing a whole philosophy on the backs of loose sheets.
stops.quote: Die Welt muss romantisirt werden. So findet man den ursprünglichen Sinn wieder.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Fragments (the programme of 'romanticizing' the world)

stops.name: Freiberg: the second betrothal, to Julie von Charpentier
stops.campa: In December, at Freiberg, life reaches again for the living: he becomes engaged a second time, to Julie von Charpentier, daughter of the mining-professor Johann von Charpentier. It is a gentler, more earthly love than the consuming vision of Sophie: a promise of an ordinary future, marriage, a career in the salt-works. He does not renounce the Night; he means to serve the Day as well. But the consumption already stirring in his lungs will not let him keep both.

segments.name: The Jena Circle: the Blue Flower and the Songs

stops.name: Weissenfels: assessor of the salt-works; the Spiritual Songs
stops.campa: His studies done, he returns to Weissenfels and is made assessor, then director, of the electoral salt-works: a serious young official who inspects mines and reckons brine, and who at his desk by candlelight writes the Geistliche Lieder, the Spiritual Songs. In them the erotic mysticism of the Night turns openly Christian: Mary, the Eucharist, the sweetness of the Redeemer. The engineer of salt is also the hymnodist of a new, tender, Romantic faith.
stops.quote: Wenn ich ihn nur habe, / Wenn er mein nur ist... / Weiß ich nichts von Leide, / Fühle nichts, als Andacht, Lieb und Freude.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Geistliche Lieder (Spiritual Songs), No. 5, first stanza
suggested_refs: Wenn ich ihn nur habe (hymn setting)

stops.name: Jena: the meeting with Ludwig Tieck; beginning Heinrich von Ofterdingen
stops.campa: In the summer he comes to Jena and meets Ludwig Tieck, and a last great friendship opens. Tieck lends him Jakob Böhme, the shoemaker-mystic; the two talk of a poetry that would make the world magical again. Fired, Novalis begins his novel Heinrich von Ofterdingen. Its young hero lies dreaming and longs, above all treasure, to behold the blaue Blume, the blue flower, the flower of infinite longing that will become the emblem of Romanticism itself, of every unappeasable desire in the world.
stops.quote: Nicht die Schätze sind es, die ein so unaussprechliches Verlangen in mir geweckt haben... aber die blaue Blume sehne ich mich zu erblicken.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Heinrich von Ofterdingen, opening chapter

stops.name: Jena, the Romantic gathering of November 1799
stops.campa: On 11 November he arrives for the famous Romantikertreffen: the gathering of the Jena circle. In the house of the Schlegels come together Friedrich and August Wilhelm Schlegel and their women Caroline and Dorothea, Ludwig Tieck, Friedrich Schelling, and Novalis. For a few electric days the founders of German Romanticism read to one another, quarrel, philosophize. Here he reads his essay Die Christenheit oder Europa, dreaming of a re-enchanted, spiritually reunited Europe, too visionary for even his friends, who advise against printing it.
stops.quote: Es waren schöne glänzende Zeiten, wo Europa ein christliches Land war, wo Eine Christenheit diesen menschlich gestalteten Welttheil bewohnte.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Die Christenheit oder Europa (Christianity or Europe), 1799

stops.name: Weissenfels, the dream of the Blue Flower written down
stops.campa: At his desk in Weissenfels he writes the opening of Heinrich von Ofterdingen. The young hero, sleepless with a stranger's tales, falls at last into a dream: a great blue flower stands by a spring, and as he bends to it the petals part and within them hovers a delicate human face. It is the beloved, it is the far-off, it is the never-attainable that draws the whole soul forward. In this single image Novalis names Romanticism itself: longing given a flower, the world made dream and the dream made world.
stops.quote: Die Welt wird Traum, der Traum wird Welt.

segments.name: The Descent into Night: Illness and Death

stops.name: Dresden, the great hemorrhage and the failed cure
stops.campa: In August 1800 he begins to cough blood; the consumption that took Sophie and Erasmus has found him. After a severe hemorrhage in November he is carried to Dresden to be treated, but the cure does not hold. He is twenty-eight, director of the salt-works, betrothed, his novel unfinished, his fame just breaking. The Night he sang toward is coming for him in earnest now, no longer a vision on a hill but a fever in the lungs, drawing him down toward the beloved he never stopped following.

stops.name: Weissenfels, the death of Novalis, 25 March 1801
stops.campa: In January he asks to be brought home to his parents' house at Weissenfels. There he lies quiet and unafraid, the dying easy as a man going toward what he has long loved. On 25 March, his brother playing the clavier softly in the next room, he falls asleep and does not wake. Friedrich Schlegel is at the bedside. He is twenty-eight. He has kept faith with the Night: the singer who called death the bride goes to her at last, unresisting, the blue flower folding shut over him.
stops.quote: Hinüber wall' ich, / Und jede Pein / Wird einst ein Stachel / Der Wollust sein.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Hymns to the Night, Fourth Hymn ('Over I journey, and every pain shall be a sting of delight')

stops.name: Alter Friedhof, Weissenfels: the grave, and the posthumous canon
stops.campa: He is buried in the Old Cemetery at Weissenfels, laid at last in the same earth of Saxony whose salts and strata he had governed. Within a year Tieck and Friedrich Schlegel gather his papers and give the world the Hymns to the Night, the Spiritual Songs, the unfinished Heinrich von Ofterdingen, the Novices of Sais. From the grave the fragments go out and multiply; the blue flower opens across a century of poets. The Night he sang keeps him, and answers every longing that will ever look up into it.
stops.quote: Zeit ist es, daß der Geist erwache... Nach oben geht der geheimnisvolle Weg.
stops.quote_source: Novalis, Fragments / Blüthenstaub ('Inward goes the mysterious way')
suggested_refs: First edition of the collected Schriften (Tieck & Schlegel, 1802)
